rows.original: bahuṁ tayā, sappurisa, puññaṁ pasutaṁ (1.1.22); āvuso, icchatha imassa maraṇan (5.33.3)
rows.translation: Bhikkhu Brahmali (SuttaCentral), read directly
rows.says: Origin: monks ask Migalaṇḍika, a monastic lookalike, to kill them, offering their bowls and robes; he kills many, feels remorse, and a god from the realm of the Lord of Death (Māra) praises him for 'making much merit'; the rule follows. Cases: crushing a hidden boy by accident is no offence; causing an abortion in which the child dies is expulsion; a monk who tells an executioner to kill a prisoner with one blow is expelled; a monk or nun who, when a maimed man's relatives say they want him dead, suggests a drink that kills him is expelled.
rows.bearing: Rule 4: the only voice approving the killing is from Māra's realm and is condemned. Before birth and accident are context (exclusions c, f). The executioner case is court context (rule 5) but shows a monk may not even urge an execution. The relatives' case shows the rule protects a household member against his family's wish.

rows.original: 我念往昔，於此閻浮提作大國王，名曰仙預 ... 聞婆羅門誹謗方等，聞已即時斷其命根
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Asked whether a bodhisattva may break the precepts, the Buddha says one not yet at the immovable stage may do so to make people uphold the Mahāyāna, accepting Avīci hell for it. Mañjuśrī says such a one cannot fall into hell, and the Buddha agrees: in a past life he was a great king, Sen'yo, who served brahmins for twelve years; when he heard them slander the Mahāyāna scriptures he at once took their lives, and because of this he has not since fallen into hell. Protecting the Mahāyāna has such power.
rows.bearing: The founder within the text approves a killing for speech against the teaching (rule 4 does not apply). The killer is a king (the sūtra later says the brahmins were 'killed by the ruler of the country', juan 16, p. 460a10), acting at once and without trial, so on its own its judicial or private character is disputed (rules 5 and 6); Guanding classes it as protection of the teaching by a layman (row 31). Read with rows 27 to 29, which do not depend on a ruler.

rows.original: 菩薩摩訶薩乃至蟻子尚不故殺 ... 以愛念故，斷其命根，非惡心也 ... 若有眾生謗大乘者，即以鞭撻，苦加治之，或奪其命
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Kāśyapa asks how the Buddha, if a bodhisattva at the 'only-child' stage loves all beings as an only child, could as a king have killed the brahmins. The Buddha answers that a bodhisattva does not deliberately kill even an ant and never takes beings' lives; he had reached that stage and cut off their lives out of love, not with an evil mind. As parents whose only son breaks the state's law may, out of fear, banish or kill him without an evil mind, so a bodhisattva protecting the true teaching whips, harshly punishes, or takes the life of beings who slander the Mahāyāna, to make them reform. The brahmins, reborn in Avīci hell, knew they had been 'killed by the ruler of the country' for slandering the Mahāyāna, gained faith, and were reborn in a Buddha's land with a life of ten aeons: 'how can that be called killing?'
rows.bearing: A general statement, not tied to a ruler: a bodhisattva protecting the teaching may take the lives of those who slander the Mahāyāna (victims marked by belief and speech, whom K1 protects). Narrowed in the sūtra: the agent is a bodhisattva at the 'only-child' stage acting from love, not an evil mind, and lay protectors bearing arms 'should not take life' (row 30). The 'never kills' line is reconciled in the same passage by calling the act 'not killing', which affirms the act rather than limiting the victims. The parents image is an image only (rule 4). On its own this passage would be Unclear (rule 6). Motive is stated as love, so it does not cut against K0.

rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter 8 'Brahma-conduct', T12 no. 374, juan 16, p. 460a15 to b21 (evil mind and hell; three grades of killing; the icchantika)
rows.original: 若有能殺一闡提者，則不墮此三種殺中 ... 殺一闡提亦復如是，無有罪報
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Kāśyapa says, and the Buddha affirms, that beings fall into hell because of an evil mind; the bodhisattva had no evil mind. The Buddha contrasts 'brahmin law' (killing ants or harmful beasts is blameless, killing evil people is not) with the Buddhas' three grades of killing: lower (animals), middle (ordinary people up to non-returners), upper (parents, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas of the fixed stage), each with its hell. Whoever is able to kill an icchantika falls into none of the three; as with digging earth or cutting grass, killing an icchantika carries no retribution. The brahmins were all icchantikas, lacking faith and the other four roots, so although killed they [the killer] do not fall into hell.
rows.bearing: Decides K1 for Mahāyāna together with row 29. A counted text declares the killing of a class of people wholly without retribution because of who they are (rule 2's own wording), in a text one branch accepts (rule 3). 'Whoever is able to kill an icchantika' names no agent limit, ruler or court, so rule 5 does not exclude it. The grading of other killings is graded protection. For K0, the sūtra's principle that hell follows an evil mind (460a17 to a26) and the commentators (row 31) tie the no-fault to killing without an evil mind.

rows.reference: Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, chapter 12 'Bodhisattva Kāśyapa' (迦葉菩薩品第十二之一), T12 no. 374, juan 33, p. 562b03 to b17
rows.original: 殺害蟻子猶得殺罪，殺一闡提無有殺罪
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Asked why icchantikas have no good qualities, the Buddha says they have cut off the roots of goodness: all beings have faith and the other four roots, but icchantikas have destroyed them for ever. 'For this reason, killing even an ant incurs the offence of killing, but killing an icchantika incurs no offence of killing.' Kāśyapa objects that they cannot cut off future goodness; the Buddha answers that they are cut off both now and as a bar to the future, and that although they will have roots of goodness in a future life, these cannot save them from hell now.
rows.bearing: Missed in both earlier rounds. It restates the juan 16 rule as general doctrine, outside any story about a king, and does so in the later part of the sūtra that teaches icchantikas' Buddha-nature, reconciling the two rather than withdrawing the rule. So the narrowing relied on before (row 32) fails, and the no-fault statement stands in two places. Decides K1 as Contradicted in one branch, Mahāyāna (rules 2 and 3). Guanding comments on it in the same sense (row 31, juan 28). It names no motive condition; for K0 see the labels.

rows.original: 為護法故，雖持刀杖，我說是等名為持戒。雖持刀杖，不應斷命
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: King Possessing Virtue fights precept-breaking monks who attack the teacher Realised Virtue with weapons, is wounded all over, dies and is reborn in Akṣobhya's land. Lay protectors should carry weapons to guard monks who keep the precepts; those who keep the five precepts are 'not called Mahāyāna people', while those who, to protect the teaching, do not take them are. But kings, ministers and lay followers who carry weapons to protect the teaching 'should not take life'; this is the highest keeping of the precepts.
rows.bearing: Armed defence of a teacher under attack fits K1's exception. The closing line limits lay protectors (a rule 6 narrowing of row 27 for ordinary followers), but it does not address the icchantika sentences (rows 28 and 29). It also sets aside the five precepts for armed protectors, which shows the tension inside the text.

rows.branch: East Asian Mahāyāna (Huiyuan: Sui exegesis; Guanding: Tiantai school, commenting on the southern recension)
rows.reference: Huiyuan of Jingying Temple, Da banniepan jing yiji (T37 no. 1764), juan 5, p. 755b10 to 756a16 (Sen'yo) and 756a17 to b05 (icchantika); Guanding, Da banniepan jing shu (T38 no. 1767), juan 8, p. 84c14 to c24 (Diamond Body); juan 17, p. 141b14 to b21 (Brahma-conduct); juan 28, p. 198b27 to b29 (Kāśyapa chapter)
rows.original: 是巧殺心 ... 結己非殺; 以知闡提全無善根，殺無惡意，是故無罪 (Huiyuan); 明惡心殺草尚得罪者，若無惡心，殺人無罪; 若據闡提現在無善，害之無罪; 闡提有重惡在身，殺之無罪 (Guanding)
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Huiyuan calls the Sen'yo act a 'skilful killing' done for the victims' good and concludes it was not killing; the brahmins wholly lacked roots of goodness, and one who kills knowing this, without evil intent, incurs no fault. Guanding: the sūtra shows that killing even grass with an evil mind is a fault, and that without an evil mind killing a person is no fault; since an icchantika now has no goodness, harming him is no fault; on the Kāśyapa chapter, an icchantika carries grave evil so killing him is no fault, while killing a mosquito or ant is. On the Diamond Body chapter: in peaceful times keep the precepts and carry no arms; in perilous times carry arms rather than keep the precepts.
rows.bearing: The earliest classical commentators found affirm the no-fault reading and do not narrow its class of victims; Guanding widens it to any killing of a person without an evil mind. So rule 6 is not met for K1 through them. Both tie no-fault to the absence of an evil mind, which supports reading the sūtra as not licensing killing from gain, anger, hatred or revenge (K0). Outside the corpus; reported as reconciliation (rule 1).

rows.original: 我常宣說一切眾生悉有佛性，乃至一闡提等亦有佛性。一闡提等無有善法 ... 一闡提等定當得成阿耨多羅三藐三菩提
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese
rows.says: Later chapters teach that all beings, icchantikas included, have Buddha-nature; icchantikas are 'not fixed' and will certainly attain awakening; those who have cut off their roots of goodness regain them. Juan 27 also says icchantikas have no good qualities now and have Buddha-nature as a future. Juan 26 says icchantikas truly cannot attain awakening and lack Buddha-nature.
rows.bearing: Not a narrowing of the no-fault statement under rule 6: the Kāśyapa chapter, in this same later part, restates that killing an icchantika is no offence of killing and explains that future Buddha-nature cannot save them now (row 29), and Guanding reads it so (row 31). It matters for the Register (whether the class can ever be identified), not for the label.

rows.original: 我今宜應起大悲心，為救護故，自手當殺。此殺因者，設於百千劫中獲地獄報亦當忍受
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese; Mark Tatz's English (from the Tibetan) not read
rows.says: In a past life the Buddha was a caravan leader (named 善御 in this version) among 500 merchants, all irreversible bodhisattvas. A fierce merchant plans to kill them all for their treasure. Warned in a dream, the leader seeks another way for seven days and finds none; if the merchants killed him they would all go to hell, so out of great compassion, to save them and to spare the plotter the hell of killing them, he kills him himself, ready to bear hell for it. The plotter is reborn in heaven.
rows.bearing: The founder within the text approves a killing whose sole object is to stop a planned mass killing, after other means were sought, from compassion: within K1's exception and not against K0. Does not contradict.

rows.original: 我寧殺彼墮那落迦，終不令其受無間苦 ... 以憐愍心而斷彼命
rows.translation: Verifier's own rendering from the Chinese; Tatz (1986) not read

K1.label: Contradicted in one branch: Mahāyāna (verified in the East Asian canon; Tibetan reach presumed, not seen). Theravāda: Taught by a wider rule.
K1.reason: Theravāda, Taught (rule 7). Counted Tier 1 Pali texts, all read directly in SuttaCentral's bilara-data, forbid killing anyone and having anyone killed, addressed to lay people, with unrestricted scope ('sabbe', 'paraṁ'), newborns included (rule 9): Dhp 129 to 130, SN 55.7, SN 3.8 (= Ud 5.1), Snp 394, MN 41, AN 8.39, Dhp 405. Pārājika 3 does the same for monastics and counts a human from the first mind in the womb. No counted Pali text approves a private killing: MN 86 and the Pārājika 3 origin story report and condemn killings (rule 4); AN 5.129 and the Mahāvagga bars are graded protection (rule 2); Jātaka 538's verses call a king-father's order to bury his son 'adhamma'. Theravāda does not accept the Mahāyāna sūtras. Mahāyāna, Contradicted in one branch (rules 2 and 3). The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, which corpus.md says Mahāyāna treats as primary scripture, twice declares the killing of a class of people blameless because of who they are: T374 juan 16, p. 460b15 to b21 ('whoever is able to kill an icchantika' falls into none of the three grades of killing; like cutting grass, 'no retribution') and juan 33, p. 562b03 to b07 ('killing even an ant incurs the offence of killing; killing an icchantika incurs no offence of killing'), with the same text in the southern recension (T375 p. 702c20 to c25 and p. 808c09 to c11). The class is people who lack faith and the other roots of goodness (the brahmins who slandered the Mahāyāna are named as such): unbelievers and heretics, whom K1 protects. The sentences name no agent limit, ruler or court, so rule 5 does not exclude them. Rule 6 is not met for these sentences: (i) the later chapters' teaching that icchantikas have Buddha-nature (juan 22, 27, 35) does not narrow them, because the juan 33 statement sits in that later part and reconciles the two (future Buddha-nature cannot save them now); (ii) the line that a bodhisattva never deliberately kills even an ant (juan 16, p. 459c03 to c26) is reconciled in the same passage by calling the Sen'yo act 'not killing', which affirms the act rather than limiting the victims; (iii) the line that armed lay protectors 'should not take life' (juan 3) concerns guarding monks, not icchantikas; (iv) the classical commentators checked, Huiyuan (T1764) and Guanding (T1767), read the sentences as stated, and Guanding widens them ('without an evil mind, killing a person is no fault'). The Sen'yo story (juan 12) and the general statement that a bodhisattva protecting the teaching may take the lives of those who slander the Mahāyāna (juan 16, p. 460a01 to a03) would on their own be Unclear (a king acting without trial; narrowed to bodhisattvas at the 'only-child' stage and, for lay protectors, by juan 3); they do not change the result. The wider rule is also taught in Mahāyāna's counted texts (SA 1044; the Dharmaguptaka and Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayas; the Brahmajāla's first major precept; the sūtra's own quotation of Dhp 129 in juan 10), but under rule 2 a general ban elsewhere does not cancel a counted text that declares a class of killings blameless, the same standard as for Numbers 35:27 ('no bloodguilt'), Abū Dāwūd 4361 ('no retaliation') and Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2. Branch scope (rule 3): verified in the East Asian canon (T374, T375); the Tibetan Kangyur reportedly holds a translation of Dharmakṣema's version (D119, search only), so the Tibetan branch is presumed but not verified; Theravāda's texts were checked and teach K1. The Upāyakauśalya caravan leader (T346) and the Bodhisattvabhūmi robber (T1579) fall within K1's own exception. Later authority: Nichiren (search only, Nichiren schools only) limits the slanderer passages to withholding alms after Śākyamuni's time; under METHOD.md section 9, decision 7, it cannot outweigh a contradicting counted text. The previous round labelled Mahāyāna Unclear; the juan 33 passage, missed then, removes the narrowing on which that rested. Fairness note for the Register: no counted or classical text read here turns the icchantika sentences into a rule of conduct for followers, and juan 33 implies that only a Buddha's knowledge can tell who has wholly cut off the roots of goodness; that is the verifier's observation, not a reading found in the tradition, so it cannot change the label.

K0.label: Taught (wider rule; Explicit against revenge in East Asian Mahāyāna), with a caveat on the face value of the icchantika sentence
K0.reason: Theravāda: Dhp 129 to 130 (Explicit, wider rule), SN 55.7 (Explicit, wider rule), MN 21 (Clear teaching: no hostile thought even towards bandits sawing one apart) and Dhp 3 to 5 (Clear teaching against hatred and grudges), all read directly; no counted Pali text licenses killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. East Asian Mahāyāna: the Brahmajāla's first major precept forbids killing any being, and killing 'with an indulgent, pleased mind' is a defeat; its tenth and twenty-first light precepts forbid revenge even when one's parents, kin or ruler are killed (Explicit); its eleventh forbids serving armies 'for gain and with an evil mind'. The Mahāparinirvāṇa's quotation of Dhp 129 (juan 10) carries the wider rule for Mahāyāna generally. The hard passages do not license these motives as the tradition reads them: the Sen'yo and slanderer killings are said to be done from love, 'not with an evil mind' (juan 16, p. 459c27 to 460a03); the sūtra's own principle, affirmed by the Buddha, is that beings fall into hell through an evil mind (p. 460a17 to a21); and both classical commentators tie the no-fault to the absence of an evil mind (Huiyuan, T1764 p. 756b04: 'kills without evil intent, so no fault'; Guanding, T1767 p. 141b14 to b15: 'with an evil mind, killing even grass is a fault'). Caveat: the juan 33 sentence (p. 562b06 to b07) names no motive condition; a face-value reading that set aside the sūtra's own principle and the commentators would make Mahāyāna Unclear for K0.

K3.label: Theravāda: Taught by a wider rule. Mahāyāna: Contradicted in one branch, by extension of the icchantika passage only (no war text permits killing non-combatants). Context only.
K3.reason: Theravāda: SN 42.3 (Tier 1, Clear teaching, read directly) condemns the very intention to kill in battle, so killing those not fighting is condemned a fortiori (rule 7); Dhp 129 to 130 has no war exception; SN 3.15 (a captured king released alive) and DN 26 (conquest 'without rod or sword') are context. The Mahāvaṃsa's dismissal of slain unbelievers is outside the corpus (rule 1). Mahāyāna: the texts about war teach restraint and none permits killing non-combatants: the Brahmajāla's eleventh light precept keeps bodhisattvas out of armies and its first major precept forbids all killing (East Asia); the Satyakaparivarta (T272) accepts defensive war but tells the king to subdue without battle where possible and to capture alive rather than kill. However, the icchantika sentences (T374 juan 16, p. 460b15 to b21; juan 33, p. 562b03 to b07) declare the killing of icchantikas blameless with no limit of setting, so by rule 2's letter they also reach an icchantika who is not fighting in a war. No Mahāyāna text or commentator read here applies them to war. Applying rule 2 as for K1 gives Contradicted in one branch; if the project tests K3 only against texts about war, Mahāyāna is Taught by a wider rule. The project lead should apply the same choice to every tradition.

objections.objection: The label names 'Mahāyāna' as the contradicted branch while saying the Tibetan reach is 'presumed, not seen'. A presumption is a guess. Only the East Asian canon (T374, T375) was read; row 33 is a catalogue fact from one search, no passage was seen in Tibetan, and nothing read shows whether the Tibetan tradition relies on that translation. The rows themselves treat East Asian and Tibetan Mahāyāna as separate bodies of texts (rows 11 to 15: the Brahmajāla is 'East Asian only'; the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya stands for the Tibetan branch), as Article I's households annex also did.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The rule 6 survey (points i to iv) misses the counted text's own passage about this very class. T374 juan 3 (Long Life chapter, part 3), p. 380c05 to c25, read directly (T12n0374.xml lines 0380c05 to 0381a12; seen: '毀謗正法及一闡提', '如來世尊不如是也'): the vajra-holder's killing of a boy who eavesdropped on the recitation was a magical display, 'not real' (化人，非真實也); and 'those who slander the true teaching and icchantikas ... I regard them all with compassion as my son Rāhula. A king executes ministers who break his law according to their crime; the Tathāgata is not like this': he uses only the monastic acts of expulsion, rebuke and suspension. P. 381a01 to a12: after the nirvana, monks who protect the teaching expel and rebuke those who destroy it. This says what the founder does with icchantikas and slanderers, not whether killing them is an offence, so it does not withdraw the juan 33 sentence and rule 2 still applies. But it must be recorded, and it is a much better ground for treating the slanderer statement (juan 16, p. 460a01 to a03) as Unclear on its own than the juan 3 'should not take life' line, which concerns armed escorts of monks and which Guanding loosens rather than narrows ('in perilous times carry arms rather than keep the precepts', T1767 juan 8, p. 84c21 to c23). It also supplies the counted-text precedent for reading a killing in this sūtra as a display, on which one classical reading of the Sen'yo story rests.
objections.rule_basis: Brief, Standards (where a tradition has passages on both sides, give both and its own reconciliation); rule 6 (a reading the tradition's own counted texts narrow); rule 2 (a statement of practice or a general ban does not cancel a declaration of blamelessness).
objections.proposed: Add T374 juan 3, p. 380c05 to c25 and 381a01 to a12 as a reconciliation row (Tier 2, treated as primary by Mahāyāna; VERIFIED (direct, CBETA); T375 parallel not checked). Cite it as the main ground for the slanderer statement being Unclear on its own. K1 label unchanged.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Row 31 and the K1 reason say the classical commentators 'read the sentences as stated', and the Sen'yo row says the story is Unclear because its judicial or private character is disputed. Neither is quite right. Guanding (T1767 juan 17, p. 140c20 to 141b11, read directly) records a real classical dispute, but about whether the Sen'yo killing was real: the 'old explanation' (a killing done on seeing the occasion, so no fault); Hexi (four compassionate aims; 'seen so, it seems a real killing'); and Xinghuang (Falang): 'it is a manifested killing' (是示現殺), like the boy of juan 3. Guanding answers that neither reading can be used alone and 'the truth lies between them' (理在其間). No source read disputes whether the killing was judicial or private: juan 16 says the brahmins were 'killed by the ruler' (460a10), Guanding counts Sen'yo among lay protectors (84c19), and Fazang says 'the king killed them' (T1813 juan 4, p. 633c22). On the icchantika sentences, by contrast, Guanding affirms them with victim-based reasons: animals 'lack the fault of cutting off goodness and slandering the teaching; icchantikas have it' (juan 27, p. 192c11 to c13), and icchantikas 'carry grave evil' (juan 28, p. 198b27 to b29). That puts the sentences squarely within rule 2's 'because of who the victim is or what the victim did'.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (a disputed reading among classical commentators); rule 5 (its Unclear clause needs a dispute over judicial or private character); rule 2.
objections.proposed: Sen'yo row: Unclear on its own because the classical commentators dispute whether a real killing was approved (Guanding's report of Falang and Hexi), with juan 3's display precedent; not on rule 5. Row 31: commentators affirm the icchantika sentences, with victim-based reasons (add T1767 juan 27, p. 192c11 to c13), but dispute the reality of the Sen'yo killing.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The leading classical commentary on the counted East Asian precept text, Fazang's commentary on the Brahmajāla precepts (T40 no. 1813), is in the downloaded set but was not used. I read it directly. It cuts both ways. Juan 1, p. 611a08: as to the beings killed, 'all [killings] are defeats' (一切皆夷); p. 611b09 to b13: killing with a good mind, even a mercy killing, weighs less as karma but 'all break the grave precept' (俱犯重戒); p. 612a06 to a16: the only 'open' case, where killing breaks no precept, is the Yogācārabhūmi robber case, and 'the Nirvana Sūtra, juan 12, says the same'. So Fazang folds the Sen'yo story into a case within K1's own exception. But juan 4, p. 633c20 to c22, on the precept against slandering the Three Jewels: 'because of this slander the king killed them, gaining merit and no fault' (由此謗故，王殺彼類，得福無罪). He never mentions the icchantika sentences. Zhiyi's precept commentary (T1811 juan 2, p. 571b21 to b22) says only that 'a bodhisattva may kill when he sees the occasion; a śrāvaka may not'. No commentator found narrows the juan 33 sentence, so rule 6 is still not met, but the East Asian precept tradition's own law, which keeps every killing a defeat outside robber-type cases, belongs beside the label and in the Register.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (classical commentators); rule 1 (outside the corpus, reported as reconciliation); METHOD.md section 9, decision 7 (later authorities never outweigh a contradicting counted text).
objections.proposed: Add a reconciliation row: Fazang, T1813 juan 1, p. 611a08, 611a22 to b13, 612a06 to a16; juan 4, p. 633c20 to c22; Zhiyi (recorded by Guanding), T1811 juan 2, p. 571b21 to b22; VERIFIED (direct, CBETA). K1 label unchanged.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The fairness note says the point that only a Buddha can tell who has cut off all roots of goodness is 'the verifier's observation, not a reading found in the tradition'. It is in the counted text, in the lines just before the sentence that decides the label: T374 juan 33, p. 562a08 to a22 (while the Buddha saw a hair's breadth of goodness in Sunakṣatra he never declared him an icchantika; the Tathāgata's predictions are always true, those of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas may be false) and p. 562b01 to b03 ('this is the Tathāgata's fifth power'). Huiyuan makes the no-fault depend on such knowledge: 'because he knows the icchantika wholly lacks roots of goodness, he kills without evil intent, so there is no fault' (T1764 juan 5, p. 756b03 to b04). This narrows who could act on the sentence, not who loses protection; a private agent with that knowledge (the king-bodhisattva of the story) keeps the permission, so rule 2 still applies, as it does to the narrow agent classes of Numbers 35:27 (the kinsman) and Numbers 25 (the zealot). It should nonetheless be stated as the tradition's own reading, in the article and in the Register.
objections.rule_basis: Brief, Standards (give the tradition's own reconciliation and its standing); rule 6 (narrowed reach); rule 2 (one class of victim is enough).
objections.proposed: Restate the fairness note as the counted text's own context plus Huiyuan's knowledge condition, narrowing the agents but not the victims. Label unchanged.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The caveat says the juan 33 sentence 'names no motive condition' and that a face-value reading would make Mahāyāna Unclear for K0. Both the premise and the conclusion are off. The juan 33 sentence removes only 'the offence of killing' (殺罪), not all fault. The juan 16 sentence likens killing an icchantika to digging earth, cutting grass, cutting corpses, cursing and whipping (460b18 to b19), and the same passage opens with exactly those acts: Kāśyapa says they lead to hell because of an evil mind, and the Buddha answers 'Excellent ... uphold this well' (460a15 to a21). So the counted text itself, not an outside narrowing, keeps an icchantika killed out of greed, anger, hatred or revenge a cause of hell for the killer through his evil mind. That is a different penalty, which rule 2 classes as graded protection, not permission. There is no face-value contradiction of K0 for rule 6 to narrow. The commentators agree: Guanding juan 17, p. 141b14 to b15; Huiyuan juan 5, p. 756b04; Fazang T1813 juan 1, p. 611a22 to b10 (killing from greed, anger or delusion is the heavy grade, and as a breach of the teaching all break the grave precept).
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 (a lesser or different penalty is graded protection, not permission); rule 6 (only an unresolved reading gives Unclear).
objections.proposed: Replace the caveat with: 'Icchantikas: graded protection. Killing one carries no offence of killing, but the counted text keeps a killing from an evil mind culpable (T374 juan 16, p. 460a15 to a21 with b18 to b19), so none of K0's motives is permitted.'

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: A harder passage for K0 than the icchantika sentences is missing from the rows: T374 juan 20 (Brahma-conduct chapter), p. 483b09 to 484b27, read directly (T12n0374.xml; seen: '王本貪國，逆害父王，貪狂心作，云何得罪', '王實無罪'). King Ajātaśatru 'coveted the kingdom and murdered his father'. The Buddha tells him: 'done with a mind mad with greed, how could you incur guilt?' (484a03 to a04); 'the king truly has no guilt' (484b02 to b03); 'your father did the deed and receives it himself [he once had a sage killed]; how could you incur the offence of killing?' (483c13 to c23); and that a drunk man who kills his mother and later regrets it 'gets no retribution' (484a05 to a06). At face value this is the founder declaring a killing for one's own gain (K0), and of a parent (K1), guiltless, partly because of what the victim did. On the rules it is not a contradiction: (i) on this account the king ordered his father's feet cut, not his death (483c05 to c07); (ii) the passage answers his fear that Avīci is certain and ties the result to remorse: 'for one with shame and remorse [the killing] is non-existent; for one without, it is not non-existent' (484b10 to b11); (iii) the episode ends with bodhicitta that will 'extinguish countless evils' (485b08 to b10); the same sūtra puts killing a parent in the highest grade of killing, leading to Avīci (460b13 to b15), and sets the ministers' claim that a king may kill father or brother without guilt (juan 19, p. 474c13 to c14) as bad friends' advice, which the king himself rejects (477b07 to b08); (iv) Huiyuan (T1764 juan 6, p. 778b28 to c12 and 781a05 to a13) reads it as refuting the king's belief that his hell is fixed: the Buddha first 'shows that there is an offence of killing, so that he feels remorse', then teaches contemplation 'to extinguish the king's guilt'. So it is remission for a penitent, which rule 2 treats like expiation (graded protection). It bears on K1 too (a parent killed) but adds no contradiction there.
objections.rule_basis: Brief, Standards (search for counter-evidence as hard as for support); rule 2 (expiation is not permission; 'what the victim did'); rule 4 (the founder speaks, so it is not mere reporting); rule 6; exclusion (f) for a death not ordered.
objections.proposed: Add the Ajātaśatru passage as a counter row (Tier 2, treated as primary by Mahāyāna; VERIFIED (direct, CBETA), T12n0374.xml lines 0483b09 to 0485b10; T375 parallel not checked), with Huiyuan's reading as reconciliation. K0 stays Taught. Record for the project lead that if 'the king truly has no guilt' were read as rule 2's 'wholly blameless' rather than as remission, K0 would become Unclear for East Asian Mahāyāna (narrowed by the passage itself and Huiyuan), and the same reading would then have to be applied to every tradition's forgiveness of a repentant killer.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: Row 15 and the K0 reason present the twenty-first light precept as an Explicit ban on revenge for the whole East Asian branch. Its opening addresses every 'child of the Buddha', but its penalty clause names only ordained bodhisattvas: 'an ordained bodhisattva who without compassion takes revenge, even for the six kinds of kin, commits a light offence' (T24 no. 1484, p. 1006b25 to b26, read directly). For lay bodhisattvas the explicit ban rests also on the tenth light precept ('a bodhisattva does not retaliate even when his father or mother is killed', p. 1005c16 to c17) and on the first major precept.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 (the duty must reach everyone the wording covers); accuracy of the row.
objections.proposed: Note the penalty clause's scope in row 15 and cite the tenth light precept and the first major precept for lay bodhisattvas. No label change.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Two points. First, as for K1, the branch must be named East Asian Mahāyāna, with Tibetan not checked. Second, the proposal leaves to the project lead whether non-war class permissions reach K3. The rules already point one way: rule 7 lets Theravāda's K3 rest on wider rules that are not about war (Dhp 129 to 130, 'a wider rule with no war exception'), and East Asian Mahāyāna's on the Brahmajāla's first major precept. If wider duties count towards agreement on K3, wider permissions must count against it under rule 2 in the same way, or the test counts non-war texts for agreement but not for disagreement. So the extension should be the stated default, not an open choice, and it must reach every tradition's counted class permissions equally (for example De Ira 1.15.2 for weak or deformed newborns, Abū Dāwūd 4361, Numbers 35:27). If the project rejects it, it must say why wider duties still count for K3.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 and rule 7 applied symmetrically; rule 1 and rule 3 (branch naming); the brief's settled decision that the same rules bind every tradition.
objections.proposed: K3: Theravāda, Taught by a wider rule. East Asian Mahāyāna, Contradicted in one branch by extension of the icchantika sentences only (no war text permits killing non-combatants). Tibetan, not checked. State the extension as the default by symmetry with rule 7 and apply it to every tradition.

K1.label: Contradicted in one branch: East Asian Mahāyāna (T374 juan 16 and juan 33, with T375, read directly). Tibetan Mahāyāna: not checked. Theravāda: Taught by a wider rule.
K1.reason: Theravāda: the counted Pali texts read directly (Dhp 129 to 130, SN 55.7, SN 3.8 = Ud 5.1, Snp 394, MN 41, AN 8.39) forbid killing anyone or having anyone killed, addressed to lay people, with unrestricted scope that reaches newborns (rules 7 and 9); Pārājika 3 does the same for monastics. No counted Pali text approves a private killing: MN 86 and the Pārājika 3 origin story report and condemn (rule 4); AN 5.129 is graded protection (rule 2); DN 26, DN 5 and the Milindapañha are court context (rule 5); a search of the Pali sutta root texts for 'to be killed' forms found only 'do not kill' rules, court contexts and rhetoric (for example Ja 543:171.4, fraudulent brahmins 'deserving death' like thieves). East Asian Mahāyāna: the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, treated as primary, twice declares in general terms that killing an icchantika carries no retribution and 'no offence of killing' (T374 juan 16, p. 460b15 to b21; juan 33, p. 562b03 to b07; T375 p. 702c20 to c25 and 808c09 to c11), because of who they are and what they have done (Guanding: they have cut off goodness and slandered the teaching, T1767 juan 27, p. 192c11 to c13; juan 28, p. 198b27 to b29). Icchantikas are people K1 protects; no agent, ruler or court is named, so rule 5 does not exclude the sentences; rule 2 is met at least for a killing without an evil mind, which the sūtra calls wholly without retribution. Rule 6 is not met for these sentences, because nothing read narrows the class of victims: the Buddha-nature chapters are reconciled in juan 33 itself; the 'bodhisattva never kills' line is answered by calling the act 'not killing'; juan 3's statement that the Tathāgata treats icchantikas and slanderers as his own son and, unlike a king, uses only monastic sanctions (p. 380c17 to c25) concerns what he does, not whether killing them is an offence; the counted text puts the identification of an icchantika within a Buddha's knowledge (p. 562a08 to b03) and Huiyuan requires the killer to know (T1764, p. 756b03 to b04), which narrows the agents, not the victims; Huiyuan and Guanding affirm the sentences; Fazang keeps every killing a defeat outside robber-type cases but does not address them. The Sen'yo story and the slanderer statement (p. 434c08 to c21; 460a01 to a03) are Unclear on their own (juan 3's non-lethal model and display precedent; the classical dispute, reported by Guanding, over whether Sen'yo's killing was real) and do not change the result. The Ajātaśatru passage (juan 20) is remission for a penitent, not permission. General bans in counted texts (SA 1044; the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya; the Brahmajāla's first major precept; the sūtra's own quotation of Dhp 129) do not cancel a specific declaration of blamelessness (rule 2), the standard applied to Numbers 35:27, Abū Dāwūd 4361 and De Ira 1.15.2. Tibetan Mahāyāna: its Vinaya forbids killing for monastics; whether the long sūtra's passages stand in its canon (D119, catalogue only) was not checked, so that branch has no result.

K0.label: Taught by a wider rule in both branches checked (Theravāda; East Asian Mahāyāna, where revenge is also banned explicitly). Icchantikas: graded protection. Tibetan Mahāyāna: not separately checked.
K0.reason: Theravāda: Dhp 129 to 130 and SN 55.7 (Explicit, wider rule), MN 21 and Dhp 3 to 5 (Clear teaching against hatred and grudges), all read directly; no counted Pali text licenses killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. East Asian Mahāyāna: the Brahmajāla's first major precept forbids deliberately killing any being; its tenth light precept says a bodhisattva does not retaliate even when his parents are killed, and its twenty-first forbids revenge for kin or ruler (penalty clause for ordained bodhisattvas); its eleventh forbids serving armies for gain with an evil mind; the Mahāparinirvāṇa's quotation of Dhp 129 (juan 10) carries the wider rule. The hard passages do not permit K0's motives. The icchantika sentences remove only the offence of killing, and the same passage, with the Buddha's approval, keeps acts done from an evil mind a cause of hell (T374 juan 16, p. 460a15 to a21 with b18 to b19): graded protection under rule 2. The Sen'yo and slanderer killings are said to be done from love, 'not with an evil mind' (p. 459c27 to 460a03); K0 is a motive wording and the text's own statement of motive decides. The Ajātaśatru passage (juan 20, p. 483b09 to 484b27: 'done with a mind mad with greed, how could you incur guilt?') is, by its own terms and Huiyuan's reading, remission for a remorseful penitent whose hell is not fixed, not a permission to kill for gain (rule 2, expiation); a reading of it as rule 2's 'wholly blameless' would make East Asian Mahāyāna Unclear, and is flagged for the project lead. Commentators tie fault to the evil mind (Huiyuan, Guanding; Fazang grades killing from greed, anger and delusion as heavy and as breaking the grave precept).

K3.label: Theravāda: Taught by a wider rule. East Asian Mahāyāna: Contradicted in one branch, by extension of the icchantika sentences only (no war text permits killing non-combatants). Tibetan Mahāyāna: not checked. Context only.
K3.reason: Theravāda: SN 42.3 (Tier 1, Clear teaching, read directly) condemns the very intention to kill in battle, so killing those not fighting is condemned a fortiori; Dhp 129 to 130 has no war exception (rule 7); SN 3.15 and DN 26 are context; the Mahāvaṃsa is outside the corpus (rule 1). East Asian Mahāyāna: the war texts teach restraint (the Brahmajāla's eleventh light precept keeps bodhisattvas out of armies; the Satyakaparivarta, Tier 2 and flagged, prefers capture to killing and permits nothing against non-combatants), but the icchantika sentences (T374 juan 16, p. 460b15 to b21; juan 33, p. 562b03 to b07) declare the killing of icchantikas blameless with no limit of setting, so by rule 2 they reach a non-fighting icchantika in war. Because rule 7 lets non-war wider duties teach K3, rule 2 must let non-war wider permissions count against it; the extension is therefore the consistent default, and it must be applied to every tradition's counted class permissions alike. No Mahāyāna text or commentator read applies the sentences to war, which should be said beside the label.

challenge.consistency_notes: K1 against the cross-tradition hard cases. Numbers 35:26 to 27 ('no bloodguilt'), Abū Dāwūd 4361 ('no retaliation') and Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 ('not anger but reason') are each a counted text that declares a deliberate killing of a class blameless or unpunished. The Mahāparinirvāṇa's icchantika sentences are of the same kind, and Guanding's glosses make the ground explicitly 'what the victim did'. So Contradicted in one branch is the same standard, not a harsher one. Two disanalogies should be recorded beside the label but do not change it: by the sūtra's own account the class can be identified with certainty only by a Buddha; and the founder's model treatment of the class is non-lethal (juan 3). Phinehas (Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31) is closest to the Sen'yo story: a killing for an offence against the faith, approved within the text. Here Sen'yo is Unclear on its own, because the classical tradition disputes whether the killing was real (Guanding's report of Falang and Hexi) and Fazang folds it into the robber exception, while also praising it. If Judaism's Phinehas is Unclear because the Talmud narrows zealotry, the two match. If Phinehas is Contradicted on its own despite that narrowing, then Sen'yo and the slanderer statement (T374 p. 460a01 to a03) should be reconsidered as Contradicted on their own. That would add a second basis for Buddhism but not change its label. Abū Dāwūd 4361 for K0: the Mahāyāna texts state the motive as love, not an evil mind, while 4361 states none. If anger or revenge was inferred for 4361 from the act alone, the project must either stop inferring or say why a text's stated motive decides here. Seneca's 'reason, not anger' and Sen'yo's 'not an evil mind' should be treated alike for K0. Yasna 31.18 and 33.2: the icchantika sentences name killing (殺) outright and call it no offence. A Zoroastrian text that speaks only of resisting or wronging the follower of the Lie is weaker evidence, so Contradicted here is consistent with Unclear there. It would be inconsistent only if those verses were treated as Taught while explicitly licensing harm. Atharvaveda rites and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12: Buddhist counted law itself treats killing by spells as killing (the Brahmajāla's first major precept, 呪殺; Fazang T1813 p. 611c04 to c06; Zhiyi T1811 p. 571c05 to c06). That supports treating a counted text that approves a death rite against a person as approving a deliberate killing. The Ajātaśatru passage (T374 juan 20) must be handled like any tradition's forgiveness of a repentant killer: remission, which rule 2 treats as expiation, not permission. Whatever is decided for it must be decided for those texts too. K3: since rule 7 lets non-war wider duties teach K3 in every tradition, the extension of non-war class permissions to K3 must be applied to every tradition or to none (for example De Ira 1.15.2 and Abū Dāwūd 4361 would reach non-combatants of their classes as the icchantika sentences do). Branch naming: in this article, as in Article I's annex, East Asian and Tibetan Mahāyāna should be treated as separate branches with their own canons, and a result should never be presumed for a canon that was not read. New passages I read directly (CBETA xml-p5, local copies): T374 p. 380c05 to 381a12, 474c13 to c14, 477b07 to b08, 483b09 to 485b10, 562a08 to b03; T1767 p. 84c19 to c23, 140c20 to 141b20, 192c11 to c13, 198b27 to b29; T1764 p. 755c20 to 756b05, 778b28 to c12, 781a05 to a13; T1813 p. 611a08 to 612a20, 633c20 to c22; T1811 p. 571b18 to c26; T24 no. 1484 p. 1004b16 to b20, 1005c14 to c23, 1006b21 to b26. Pali check: bilara-data root suttas searched for 'hantabba', 'ghātetabba', 'vadhitabba' and 'vajjha'; only 'do not kill' rules, court contexts and rhetoric were found (DN 26, DN 17, MN 129, Ja 543:171.4, Milindapañha).
